summary: A 1970 note commenting on the protocol described in RFC 36. It updates RFC 36 with feedback from the RAND authors. It is one of the discussion contributions in the early protocol design process.

plainLanguage.summary: This note proposes extra commands for the protocol described in RFC 36, including ways to report errors and ask about connections. The authors also warn that the connection setup seems complex and may need more study.

subtitle: RAND's suggested additions and concerns about the protocol described in RFC 36.

tldr.problem: The authors wanted added ways to report protocol errors, query connection status, terminate program connections and signal host status.
tldr.mechanism: They propose new commands for errors, queries, termination, host status, unicast transmission and broadcast, while criticizing the complexity of connection setup.
tldr.outcome: The suggestions were offered for consideration in later grammar specifications; the authors say the connection problem needed more study.
tldr.outcomeLabel: A proposal, not a final design

sections.title: Suggested Protocol Additions
sections.content: E. Harslem and J. Heafner offer suggestions for additions to the April 28, 1970 protocol grammar discussed in RFC 36. They describe the commands as suggestions, not a completed design.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors suggest extra commands for a protocol draft. Their note is feedback for later specifications, not a final protocol.

sections.title: Error Messages and Connection Queries
sections.content:
The proposed <ERR> message includes an error class and the command that caused the error. The three classes are content errors, status errors, and resource allocation or exhaustion. The code identifies the class and offending item, while the command is returned to the sending Network Control Program (NCP) for analysis.

The proposed <QRY> command asks a remote NCP for connection status. A query with a zero My Socket asks for the status of all connections to a remote host. The authors say queries could provide limited error recovery without reinitializing an NCP.
sections.plainLanguage: An error reply would identify what kind of problem occurred and return the failed command. A query would let one NCP ask another about connection status.

sections.title: Termination, Host Status and Message Delivery
sections.content:
The proposed <TER> command closes all connections between a program and the programs at a host, supplementing rather than replacing <CLS>. The <HCU> and <HGD> messages report that a host is coming up or voluntarily going down.

The proposed <TRN> prefix sends a message body to one process. The <BDC> prefix asks the destination NCP to distribute the body over receiving connections linked to the sender. These messages use links assigned to user programs rather than the control link.
sections.plainLanguage: The suggestions include one command to close several connections and signals for host startup or shutdown. They also distinguish a message for one process from one distributed to linked connections.

sections.title: Concern About Connection Complexity
sections.content:
The authors criticize the request-for-connection and dynamic-reconnection design as complex, with many control messages and queues imposed by the protocol. They say it does not account for a situation where only a controlling process knows that a subordinate process should be contacted during dynamic reconnection.

They clarify that the criticism is not meant to delay changes or criticize the people who planned them. They had not studied the problem in depth and say it deserves more study after the current specifications have been exercised.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors worry that connection setup uses too many steps and may affect response time. They say more study is needed after people try the current specification.

references.text: The protocol whose grammar specifications the authors propose to extend.
